record.title: A preprint reports that retrieving long simulator output can divert agents from authoritative evidence
record.summary: In an Oct 19 arXiv preprint, authors report that how tool results are delivered changed answer accuracy in PHREEQC agent tasks. Across 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items, table-of-contents retrieval rather than inline report delivery was associated with an 11.3-point drop for GPT-5.1; GPT-5.2’s reported 7.9-point drop was not significant after Holm correction. Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 showed no detectable net effect. The authors traced some errors to agents answering from higher-precision output files instead of the simulator report, and report that naming the authoritative report improved results in intervention runs. These are author-reported results in one deterministic scientific simulator, not an independent reproduction or evidence of a general retrieval penalty.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_PUBLIC_ARTIFACT
claims.text: arXiv records v1 of this paper as submitted 19 October 2026.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that table-of-contents retrieval of PHREEQC reports, instead of inline output, lowered accuracy by 11.3 percentage points for GPT-5.1 (95% item-bootstrap interval −18.0 to −4.9; Holm-corrected p=0.005) and by 7.9 points for GPT-5.2 (interval −14.9 to −0.9; Holm-corrected p=0.128, not significant after correction). They report no detectable net effect for Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 or GPT-5.4.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that the models produced the keyed simulator values at similar rates, but under retrieval sometimes answered from their own higher-precision output files instead of the simulator report and selected a neighboring multiple-choice option. They call this “evidence substitution.”

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper’s intervention runs, an instruction to answer from the simulator report reduced report-skipping to under 2% and raised closure to 99%; inline delivery of outputs that fit had a similar effect, while a rounding instruction alone did not.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_SOURCE_LIMITATION
claims.text: The paper studies one deterministic geochemistry simulator (PHREEQC) and 158 retained items from 19 setups. It reports execution-based verification of the keys and offline replay of logged simulator calls, but the paper does not establish transfer to other tools, domains, harnesses or model settings.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent group has reproduced the reported accuracy effects, evidence-substitution mechanism or interventions.
The evaluation uses one simulator, a narrow task format, closed API models and differing run/prompt conditions; transfer to other long-output tools and natural agent tasks is unknown.
For GPT-5.2, the reported retrieval effect is not significant after Holm correction across five models; some conditions have limited repeats, and models were served at different times.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported mechanism generalizes to other long-output agent tools, harness designers may need to preserve authoritative tool evidence explicitly because retrieval can change what evidence agents use even when the underlying simulator computes the correct value. The current result is one author-run PHREEQC regime with a limited model set, so broader deployment and economic impact remain unmeasured.
limitations: The reported study is a preprint and its experimental results have not been independently reproduced in this review.

The task regime is 158 execution-verified PHREEQC multiple-choice questions from one scientific simulator. The authors excluded defective items from a 200-item pool and report that conclusions are similar on a stricter 134-item subset.

The reported accuracy change differs by model. GPT-5.1’s result is significant after the paper’s Holm correction; GPT-5.2’s result does not meet that corrected threshold. Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 show no detectable net change.

The paper uses closed models and API defaults for GPT; conditions differ in tool-description prompts, repeat counts are incomplete, and full-agent runs occurred at different times. The authors do not determine which model property drives the differences.
The findings do not establish that file retrieval generally reduces agent accuracy or that the observed mechanism transfers to other domains, tools or production harnesses.
brief.summary: In an Oct 19 arXiv preprint, authors report that how tool results are delivered changed answer accuracy in PHREEQC agent tasks. Across 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items, table-of-contents retrieval rather than inline report delivery was associated with an 11.3-point drop for GPT-5.1; GPT-5.2’s reported 7.9-point drop was not significant after Holm correction. Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 showed no detectable net effect. The authors traced some errors to agents answering from higher-precision output files instead of the simulator report, and report that naming the authoritative report improved results in intervention runs. These are author-reported results in one deterministic scientific simulator, not an independent reproduction or evidence of a general retrieval penalty.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report a retrieval-associated accuracy loss for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 on PHREEQC tasks, with the corrected GPT-5.2 result not statistically significant; three other analyzed models show no detectable net change.
technical.compute_or_cost: The study does not establish a general cost or efficiency advantage for retrieval. Any context savings must be evaluated alongside model-specific accuracy and evidence-use behavior.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public arXiv preprint documents the authors’ experimental protocol and reported results. The key numbers and mechanism remain author-reported rather than independently replicated here.
technical.mechanism: Agents run PHREEQC and receive either a simulator report inline or a table-of-contents index for reading selected report ranges. Under retrieval, some GPT agents reportedly answered from their own higher-precision output files instead of the simulator report and rounded to a neighboring option. An instruction to use the report or inline output that fits reduced this behavior in the reported intervention runs.
technical.regime: One deterministic aqueous-geochemistry simulator, 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items from 19 PHREEQC setups, six API model families, several output-delivery conditions and incomplete repeats. The authors report one shared run on 33 long-output items and different model/run times.
technical.reproducibility: The paper reports execution-based answer-key checks, logs and offline reruns of 11,007 simulator calls. This review did not independently reproduce model/API trials; API snapshots, prompts, repetitions and transfer conditions remain limitations.
technical.strongest_baseline: Within each model, table-of-contents retrieval is compared with inline simulator output; paired replay for GPT-5.2 holds the simulation result fixed and changes only delivery for the analyzed checkpoints.

brief.title: A preprint reports that retrieving long simulator output can divert agents from authoritative evidence
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported mechanism generalizes, an agent can compute the right result yet answer from a less authoritative copy when long tool output is stored for later retrieval. That could affect choices about how harnesses expose logs, search results and simulator reports. The paper tests one simulator and shows different effects across models, so it does not justify a general rule against retrieval.
